Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LAKE WALES, Florida (CNN) -- Does jumping out of a plane show love? For one family in Florida it does. Trevor Muir (left), 23; Darcy Shepard, 18; Harriett Shepard, 94; and Dave Shepard, 74, are ready to jump. Last Saturday, four generations of Darcy Shepard's family went skydiving for her 18th birthday. The oldest jumper was Shepard's 94-year-old great-grandmother, Harriett Shepard. Skydiving is becoming a Shepard family rite of passage. Two members of the family had jumped before -- including family matriarch Harriett. Harriett Shepard jumped three years ago, at age 91, because she wanted to know what it felt like. She is an inspiration to her great-granddaughter. "If she can do it at 91, then I could, too," Darcy says, explaining that she wasn't allowed to jump three years ago because she hadn't reached age 18. As Darcy planned the adventure, her brother, cousins, father and grandfather decided to join her in skydiving. At first, the family invited 94-year-old Harriett to watch everyone skydive in central Florida. But Harriett, known to the family as "Honeynun," didn't want to watch. She wanted to jump.  Watch Harriett and kin soar across the sky » . Adventure isn't new to this bunch. In the past the family has gone scuba diving and hang gliding together. Jumping out of the plane were Harriett; Darcy; Harriett's 74-year-old son Dave; Dave's 45-year-old son Dallas, who is Darcy's dad; two cousins; a girlfriend; and a future father-in-law. As she suited up, Harriett said she found it "exciting to be doing this with the family." The eight uncertified skydivers were trained and paired with tandem instructors at Florida Skydiving Center at the Lake Wales Airport. The center required Harriett to be cleared by a doctor prior to jumping. Florida Skydiving says Harriett Shepard is the oldest person to jump at the center. As jump time nears, Harriett is fearless. "I'm never scared up there," she says. "My husband and I had a plane. I'm never afraid."  See photos of the family's skydiving day » . Great-grandson Trevor Muir, another of the jumpers, says he has water-skied, jumped on a trampoline and climbed giant tree forts with his great-grandmother. "So what's skydiving? Just another notch in the pole," says the 23-year-old Trevor. "We've done a lot of crazy things." The plane, a DeHavilland Twin Otter, takes the group to an altitude of 14,000 feet. The rear door opens. Pilot Eric Weaver announces over the radio: "Attention any traffic in the Lake Wales area. There will be skydiving over the Lake Wales Airport." First to jump is 94-year-old Harriett, with her instructor David "Pip" Perry. The skydivers free-fall at speeds between 120 and 150 mph before deploying their parachute. "Honeynun" slowly floats to the ground, wearing her cozy buckle-up sandals that she feels are more comfortable than closed-toe shoes. After landing, Harriett -- who has battled skin cancer -- is more fearful of the sun than jumping from the plane. One skydiver after the other lands safely to fanfare from anxious family members on the ground. Eighteen-year-old Darcy is greeted with a chorus of "Happy Birthday." There are lots of high-fives, family photos and exclamations of "awesome." Darcy hugs her great-grandmom: "Yay, Honeynun." Darcy's father, Dallas Shepard, deems it "an incredible jump that was a lot of fun." Dallas says that skydiving with his grandmother was "kind of neat, just being able to do it with her -- but she is living life, and that's the best part." His father, Dave Shepard, calls it an experience he will remember for a long time. "It was something special, where we had four generations." Harriett Shepard confesses that her late husband would not be happy. "He would have never let me do this," she says. "He took care of me -- that's why I'm this old." Yet Harriett, who has lived a long and full life as an author, photographer and architect, is concerned about the publicity. "She's worried," Dave Shepard says of his mom, "that the only thing people will remember her for is jumping out of an airplane."

Trevor Muir, 23; Darcy Shepard, 18; Harriett Shepard, 94; and Dave Shepard, 74, prepare to jump.

Last Saturday, four generations of Darcy Shepard’s family went skydiving to celebrate her 18th birthday. The oldest participant was Shepard’s 94-year-old great-grandmother, Harriett Shepard.

Skydiving is becoming a rite of passage for the Shepard family. Two family members had jumped before, including its matriarch, Harriett. She first went skydiving three years ago, at age 91, because she wanted to know what it felt like.

She is an inspiration to her great-granddaughter.

“If she can do it at 91, then I could, too,” Darcy says, explaining that she was not allowed to jump three years ago because she had not yet turned 18.

As Darcy planned the adventure, her brother, cousins, father and grandfather decided to join her. Initially, the family invited 94-year-old Harriett to watch everyone skydive in central Florida. But Harriett, known to the family as “Honeynun,” did not want to watch. She wanted to jump.

*Watch Harriett and her family soar across the sky »*

Adventure is nothing new for this group. In the past, the family has gone scuba diving and hang gliding together.

Those jumping from the plane included Harriett; Darcy; Harriett’s 74-year-old son, Dave; Dave’s 45-year-old son, Dallas, who is Darcy’s father; two cousins; a girlfriend; and a future father-in-law.

As she suited up, Harriett said she found it “exciting to be doing this with the family.”

The eight uncertified skydivers received training and were paired with tandem instructors at the Florida Skydiving Center at Lake Wales Airport. The center required Harriett to obtain medical clearance before jumping. According to Florida Skydiving, Harriett Shepard is the oldest person ever to jump at the center.

As jump time approaches, Harriett remains fearless.

“I’m never scared up there,” she says. “My husband and I had a plane. I’m never afraid.”

*See photos of the family’s skydiving day »*

Great-grandson Trevor Muir, another of the jumpers, says he has water-skied, bounced on a trampoline and climbed giant tree forts with his great-grandmother.

“So what’s skydiving? Just another notch in the pole,” says 23-year-old Trevor. “We’ve done a lot of crazy things.”

A DeHavilland Twin Otter carries the group to an altitude of 14,000 feet. The rear door opens, and pilot Eric Weaver announces over the radio: “Attention any traffic in the Lake Wales area. There will be skydiving over the Lake Wales Airport.”

The first to jump is 94-year-old Harriett, accompanied by her instructor, David “Pip” Perry. The skydivers free-fall at speeds ranging from 120 to 150 mph before deploying their parachutes.

“Honeynun” floats slowly to the ground, wearing her comfortable buckle-up sandals, which she finds more comfortable than closed-toe shoes.

After landing, Harriett—who has battled skin cancer—is more concerned about the sun than she is about jumping from an airplane.

One by one, the skydivers land safely, greeted with fanfare from anxious family members waiting on the ground. Eighteen-year-old Darcy is welcomed with a chorus of “Happy Birthday.” High-fives, family photographs and exclamations of “awesome” abound.

Darcy embraces her great-grandmother. “Yay, Honeynun.”

Darcy’s father, Dallas Shepard, describes it as “an incredible jump that was a lot of fun.”

Dallas says skydiving with his grandmother was “kind of neat, just being able to do it with her—but she is living life, and that’s the best part.”

His father, Dave Shepard, calls it an experience he will remember for a long time.

“It was something special, where we had four generations.”

Harriett Shepard acknowledges that her late husband would not have been happy.

“He would have never let me do this,” she says. “He took care of me—that’s why I’m this old.”

Yet Harriett, who has lived a long and full life as an author, photographer and architect, is concerned about the publicity.

“She’s worried,” Dave Shepard says of his mother, “that the only thing people will remember her for is jumping out of an airplane.”

**LAKE WALES, Florida (CNN) —** Can parachuting from an aircraft be a way to express affection? For one Florida family, the answer is yes.

Trevor Muir, 23; Darcy Shepard, 18; Harriett Shepard, 94; and Dave Shepard, 74, were among those preparing to take the plunge. Last Saturday, relatives representing four generations celebrated Darcy’s 18th birthday by skydiving together. The oldest participant was her 94-year-old great-grandmother, Harriett.

The activity is beginning to resemble a coming-of-age tradition in the Shepard family. Two relatives had already skydived, including Harriett, the family matriarch. She made her first jump three years earlier, when she was 91, simply because she wanted to experience it.

Her example motivated Darcy.

“If she can do it at 91, then I could, too,” Darcy said. She explained that she had wanted to join Harriett three years ago but was not permitted because she was younger than 18.

While Darcy organized her birthday outing, her father, grandfather, brother and cousins chose to participate as well. Initially, the family asked Harriett—affectionately called “Honeynun” by her relatives—to come to central Florida and watch. Watching, however, was not enough for her; she wanted to go up and jump with everyone else.

A video showed Harriett and her relatives flying through the sky.

Adventurous group activities are nothing unusual for this family. They have previously gone scuba diving and hang gliding together.

The eight people who exited the plane were Harriett; Darcy; Harriett’s 74-year-old son, Dave; Dave’s 45-year-old son and Darcy’s father, Dallas; two cousins; a girlfriend; and a future father-in-law.

While putting on her equipment, Harriett described sharing the experience with her relatives as “exciting.”

None of the eight held skydiving certification, so the Florida Skydiving Center at Lake Wales Airport provided training and matched each one with a tandem instructor. Before Harriett could participate, the facility required approval from a physician. According to Florida Skydiving, she is the oldest person ever to jump at that center.

As departure time approached, Harriett showed no fear.

“I’m never scared up there,” she said. “My husband and I had a plane. I’m never afraid.”

Photos documented the family’s day of skydiving.

Another jumper, Harriett’s 23-year-old great-grandson Trevor Muir, said the two of them had already shared many activities, including water-skiing, bouncing on a trampoline and climbing enormous tree forts.

“So what’s skydiving? Just another notch in the pole,” Trevor said. “We’ve done a lot of crazy things.”

A DeHavilland Twin Otter carried the family to 14,000 feet. When the aircraft’s rear door opened, pilot Eric Weaver broadcast a warning over the radio: “Attention any traffic in the Lake Wales area. There will be skydiving over the Lake Wales Airport.”

Harriett was the first family member out of the plane. She jumped in tandem with instructor David “Pip” Perry. During free fall, the participants reached speeds ranging from 120 to 150 mph before opening their parachutes.

Known to her family as Honeynun, Harriett drifted gently back to earth in comfortable, buckled sandals, which she prefers to closed-toe footwear. Afterward, Harriett—who has fought skin cancer—appeared more worried about exposure to the sun than about leaping from an aircraft.

Every jumper landed without incident as nervous relatives waiting below celebrated. When Darcy touched down, the crowd welcomed her with a rendition of “Happy Birthday.” High-fives, group pictures and repeated cries of “awesome” followed.

Darcy embraced her great-grandmother and cheered, “Yay, Honeynun.”

Dallas Shepard, Darcy’s father, characterized the outing as “an incredible jump that was a lot of fun.” He said sharing the experience with his grandmother was “kind of neat, just being able to do it with her—but she is living life, and that’s the best part.”

Dallas’ father, Dave Shepard, said the occasion would remain in his memory for years. To him, its importance came from having four generations take part together.

Harriett acknowledged that her deceased husband would have objected to the adventure.

“He would have never let me do this,” she said. “He took care of me—that’s why I’m this old.”

Despite a rich and lengthy life that has included work as an author, photographer and architect, Harriett has mixed feelings about the attention generated by her jump.

Dave said his mother fears “that the only thing people will remember her for is jumping out of an airplane.”
